topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: HCl in the stomach denatures proteins, activates pepsinogen to pepsin, and kills most ingested bacteria (bactericidal role, pH 1–2). Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes throughout the body and is not a function of HCl.

options.text: Denaturing proteins to expose peptide bonds for digestion
Synthesizing new proteins for muscle growth

stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the stomach relevant to defence against pathogens?

topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: Goblet cells in the respiratory tract secrete mucus, a thick sticky fluid that physically traps airborne microbes and particles. Cilia then sweep the mucus (with trapped pathogens) toward the pharynx, this is the mucociliary escalator.

options.text: By producing high-voltage electrical impulses that repel microbes
Through secretion of a viscous fluid (mucus) that physically traps microorganisms
By releasing phagocytic cells into the airway lumen
By increasing local temperature to destroy pathogens

stem: How do the mucous membranes of the respiratory tract trap airborne pathogens?

topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: Keratin is a tough, fibrous, waterproof protein that fills the dead cells of the epidermis, making the skin mechanically resistant and impenetrable to most microorganisms.

options.text: Provide a nutrient source for beneficial skin bacteria
Create a waterproof and tough physical barrier against microbial entry
Signal the second line of defence when damaged
Neutralize acidic toxins produced by pathogens

stem: The presence of keratin in the outer layer of human skin primarily serves to:

topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: Lysozyme cleaves the glycosidic bonds in peptidoglycan, a component of bacterial cell walls. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick, exposed peptidoglycan layer, making them more susceptible to lysozyme than Gram-negative bacteria, viruses, protozoa, or fungi.
stem: Lysozyme, found in tears and saliva, is most effective against which type of microorganism?

topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: Sebum contains fatty acids and sweat contains lactic acid/salts that lower skin pH to approximately 3–5, chemically inhibiting bacterial growth. Stratified epithelium and cilia are physical/mechanical barriers; urine flushing is a mechanical barrier.

options.text: Intact stratified squamous epithelium of the skin
Low pH of sebum and sweat on the skin surface

stem: Which of the following is considered a CHEMICAL barrier in the first line of defence?

topicTitle: 9.1 First Line of Defence
explanation: Skin and mucous membranes are external barriers that inhibit microbial invasion before internal immune responses are required.
stem: Which is part of the first line of defence?

topicTitle: 9.2 Second Line of Defence: Nonspecific Defence
explanation: The complement system is a cascade of plasma proteins. When activated, complement proteins assemble into the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) that inserts into the bacterial cell membrane, creating pores that cause osmotic lysis and bacterial death.
stem: The Membrane Attack Complex (MAC), which punches holes in bacterial cell membranes causing lysis, is formed by activation of which system?

topicTitle: 9.2 Second Line of Defence: Nonspecific Defence
explanation: Interferons are proteins secreted by virus-infected cells that signal neighbouring healthy cells to produce antiviral proteins, inhibiting viral replication in those cells. This is a nonspecific defence that limits the spread of any virus.
stem: Which antimicrobial protein warns uninfected neighbouring cells to produce antiviral defences, limiting viral spread?

topicTitle: 9.2 Second Line of Defence: Nonspecific Defence
explanation: Histamine released by mast cells and damaged cells causes vasodilation and increases capillary permeability. Plasma fluid, proteins, and clotting factors leak into the interstitial space, causing the characteristic swelling (edema) of inflammation.

options.text: Decreased blood flow to the area
Increased permeability of capillaries due to histamine
The accumulation of red blood cells at the injury site
The release of interferons by mast cells

stem: During an inflammatory response, what is the primary cause of localized edema (swelling)?

topicTitle: 9.2 Second Line of Defence: Nonspecific Defence
explanation: A moderate fever inhibits the growth and reproduction of many bacteria (which have optimal growth at normal body temperature) and increases the metabolic rate of host immune cells, accelerating phagocytosis and tissue repair.

options.text: It denatures the host's enzymes to stop metabolism
It increases the rate of bacterial binary fission
It inhibits bacterial growth and speeds up phagocytosis by immune cells
It prevents the release of pyrogens from microbes

stem: What is the physiological benefit of a moderate fever during a bacterial infection?

topicTitle: 9.2 Second Line of Defence: Nonspecific Defence
explanation: The canonical text identifies macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils as the main phagocytic white blood cells.
stem: Which cells are main types of phagocytic white blood cells?

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: Unlike the innate (non-specific) first and second lines, the adaptive immune system (third line) is highly specific to particular pathogens and generates memory cells that enable a faster, stronger response upon re-exposure, the hallmarks of specific immunity.

options.text: It is present from birth and is innate.
It involves physical barriers such as the skin.
It exhibits immunological memory and high specificity for particular antigens.
It utilises inflammation as its primary mechanism.

stem: Which feature distinguishes the third line of defence (specific immunity) from the first and second lines of defence?

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: Helper T-cells secrete interleukins, a class of cytokines that act as chemical messengers to activate and coordinate both B-cells (antibody-mediated immunity) and Cytotoxic T-cells (cell-mediated immunity). Perforins are used by cytotoxic T-cells; histamines are released in allergic responses.
stem: Which chemical signals are released by Helper T-cells ($T_H$ cells) to stimulate the proliferation of B-cells and Cytotoxic T-cells?

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: B-lymphocytes are the key cells of humoral immunity. Upon activation, they undergo clonal selection and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete large quantities of specific antibodies into the blood and lymph.
stem: Which type of lymphocyte is primarily responsible for the humoral (antibody-mediated) immune response?

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: An epitope (also called an antigenic determinant) is the specific molecular site on an antigen that is recognised by the variable region (paratope) of an antibody. This lock-and-key specificity is fundamental to the adaptive immune response.
stem: The specific region on an antigen that is recognised and bound by an antibody is called the:

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: During the primary response, clonal selection produces long-lived memory cells. Upon re-exposure to the same antigen, these memory cells bypass the initial lag phase and rapidly proliferate and differentiate, producing a faster and larger antibody response.

options.text: The skin becomes more impermeable to the pathogen.
Memory B and T cells are already present and can rapidly recognise the antigen.
The pathogen becomes weaker after the first infection.
Phagocytosis is suppressed, allowing antibodies to act faster.

stem: During a secondary immune response, why is the reaction faster and more intense than the primary response?

topicTitle: 9.3 Third Line of Defence: Specific Defences
explanation: The specific immune response has humoral and cell-mediated forms carried out by B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes.
stem: Which cells carry out the two main types of specific immune response?

topicTitle: 9.4 Types of Acquired Immunity
explanation: Active immunity (both natural and artificial) stimulates the host's immune system to produce its own antibodies and memory cells, ensuring long-term recognition and faster secondary responses.
stem: Which type of immunity is characterized by the production of memory B and T cells?

topicTitle: 9.4 Types of Acquired Immunity
explanation: Recovery from a natural infection leads to Natural Active Immunity because the body's own immune system responded to the live pathogen and formed memory cells.
stem: A person who has recovered from mumps develops a lifelong resistance to the virus. This is an example of:

topicTitle: 9.4 Types of Acquired Immunity
explanation: Since the antibodies are pre-formed by the mother and transferred naturally via breast milk (colostrum), it is classified as Natural Passive Immunity, no immune response is triggered in the newborn.
stem: The transfer of IgA antibodies through colostrum to a newborn provides which type of protection?

topicTitle: 9.4 Types of Acquired Immunity
explanation: Passive immunity provides ready-made antibodies. Because the recipient's immune system is not challenged by antigens, no memory cells are formed, and protection fades once the injected antibodies are degraded.

options.text: It does not stimulate the recipient's B-cells to produce memory cells.
The antibodies are destroyed by stomach acid.
It only contains antigens, not antibodies.
It relies on the slow activation of T-cells.

stem: Why is the protection offered by an anti-tetanus serum (ATS) injection considered temporary?

topicTitle: 9.4 Types of Acquired Immunity
explanation: Vaccination introduces antigen to stimulate the body to manufacture antibodies, producing artificial active immunity.
stem: What is vaccination an example of?
